newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Hungary's health care in parlous state.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hungary's health care in parlous state.

text.p: Margit Dinnyes, who uses a walker to get around, is one of the patients to be evicted when a century-old hospital in Budapest shuts its doors this month.

"It's a big mistake to be getting rid of 10,000 hospital beds when they are needed," said Dinnyes, a frail 91-year-old who does not know where she will go when Balassa Janos hospital in the seedy Eighth District closes under a restructuring plan.

Hungary's socialist-led government, saddled with social security deficits $300 million more than agreed with the International Monetary Fund, says it must cut 10,000 of the country's more than 90,000 hospital beds to slash costs and bring down the soaring deficit.
But the cuts are being made at a time when the health care system in Hungary is in chaos and the overall state of health of its 10 million people is among the worst in Europe.

Average life expectancy for Hungarian males aged 35 to 69 is the lowest in Europe. Half the men in that age group are not expected to live to 70. Some 21 percent will succumb to lung cancer linked to smoking, according to statistics provided by the World Bank. One in five males is an alcoholic, according to a Central Statistical Office survey.

Rates of cardiovascular disease, fuelled in part by Hungary's cholesterol-rich diet, are among the highest in Europe. Deaths from cirrhosis are soaring while alcoholism, hypertension and depression all contribute to the high morbidity and mortality rates.
HIGHEST MORTALITY RATES IN EUROPE

"Hungary has the highest mortality rates in Europe, and especially in the age group of males 35 to 64," said Dr Ivan Gyarfas, a cardiologist who is a coordinator in the Ministry of Welfare for a World Bank-backed health management project.
"There are excessive numbers of deaths in this group and these are due to cardiovascular diseases, stroke and coronary heart disease," Gyarfas told Reuters.

Moreover, despite having some 160 hospitals, teaching institutions and similar facilities, the average level of health within communities varies wildly from one part of the country to another, and from one part of a city to the next.
"Life expectancy in (Budapest's wealthy) Second and Twelfth Districts is the same as in the Netherlands," said Balazs Rekassy, also a coordinator for the World Bank project.
"In the Eighth District it is like Sub-Saharan Africa."

The parlous state of Hungary's health care system was highlighted by the resignation last month of Health Minister Gyorgy Szabo. He had come under heavy pressure to approve a health budget which hospital officials said did not keep abreast of the country's 20 percent a year inflation.
The government has taken weeks to name a successor.
It has had to provide stopgap funding after hospitals said that, unless debts were settled, 49 hospitals would run out of blood plasma and medicines.

Dr Gyula Kovecs, president of the Hungarian Hospital Association, said cuts so far had not saved money and succeeded only in further demoralising staff, such as nurses who are paid about 35,000 forints ($225) a month.

"We do need a reform but let's start from the beginning. In countries like Britain, France and Switzerland they calculate $2,000 per person (for health care) while in Hungary we are at about $300," Kovecs told Reuters.

"It is true that there are too many hospitals and too many hospital beds, but the people of Hungary were educated and born with the notion that there is only one place to get cured and this is in a hospital."
Kovecs said his association planned to liaise with patients' associations and health products providers, including drug and equipment manufacturers, to lobby the government.
"We would like to be at least as strong as the energy or monetary lobby," he said. "We do not want them just to throw us around as they do now."
But bringing the health of Hungarians up to first world levels may prove difficult if the experience of the World Bank-backed health management project is a gauge.
HEALTH MANAGEMENT PROJECT
After several years of planning, the bank approved a loan of $92 million for an overall $130 million project to upgrade and reform health care and health care management in Hungary.
The project, the biggest of its kind in the region, is also one of the biggest problem programmes in the region, according to Guy Ellena, a World Bank senior health economist.

"To give you an order of magnitude, this loan was $92 million and today, after three years, the disbursement is about $15 million," Ellena said in an interview. "That's all, and even this is a very last figure."

Ellena said it usually takes time for programmes to get off the ground, but the delays in Hungary have been excessive. One of the biggest projects, to introduce computerised information systems into hospitals plagued by bureaucratic procedures left over from communist times, simply never got started.

"This was one of the reasons why the project was so poorly rated on our side," Ellena said. He said the bank and the government agreed that having the ministry oversee this project for decentralised hospitals didn't work and the hospitals were now going to try to do it themselves.

"It's not unusual altogether (that) projects perform better or worse but, that being said, Hungary is a country which is on the higher part of the middle-income economies and has big expectations of joining the EU quickly," Ellena said.
"So if Hungary cannot do that well, then Hungary does not have the strength of its own ambitions."
